Lumbar disk protrusion

High-intensity laser added to spinal decompression improved disability, lumbar flexion, and straight-leg raising at two weeks, but did not significantly reduce back or radiating-leg pain versus decompression alone. In a related herniation trial, low-level laser was similar to placebo on several outcomes.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

High-intensity laser added to spinal decompression improved disability, lumbar flexion, and straight-leg raising at two weeks, but did not significantly reduce back or radiating-leg pain versus decompression alone. In a related herniation trial, low-level laser was similar to placebo on several outcomes.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact category contains one 63-person human randomized trial of high-intensity laser therapy, or HILT, added to spinal decompression. A narrowly mapped study of lumbar disc herniation adds one related trial of low-level laser, LED, and placebo, but it does not directly study the protrusion label. These are two distinct trials, and the mapped item is not treated as direct evidence.

Human and clinical evidence

Chen and colleagues found that HILT plus spinal decompression improved Oswestry Disability Index scores, lumbar flexion, and straight-leg raising more than decompression alone after two weeks. Back pain and radiating-leg pain did not show a significant between-group difference. HILT is a high-intensity intervention and does not represent standard low-power PBM. In the related lumbar-herniation trial, low-level laser was similar to placebo for several outcomes while LED performed better on some pain and function measures; all groups also received positioning and exercise (Chen et al. 2018 de Carvalho et al. 2016).

Animal evidence

No relevant animal study was identified.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone cell or tissue experiment was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The direct trial used 1064 nm near-infrared HILT, delivered in three phases with a total of 7500 J and reported fluence of 150 J/cm² over a 1 cm² spot, across ten sessions in two weeks. Its results apply to HILT combined with decompression, not to PBM alone. The mapped study used 904 nm laser and 945 nm LED alongside exercises, adding further intervention differences.

Interpretation

The direct trial supports short-term functional improvement from an adjunctive HILT regimen, while its pain outcomes were not significantly better. Evidence for low-power PBM in this exact indication remains indirect and uncertain.

Evidence strength in source summaryShort-term function after adjunctive high-intensity laser: Low Pain after high-intensity laser: Very low Low-level laser for related lumbar herniation: Very low
Publications and records2 unique mapped titles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The direct 63-person trial found short-term improvement in selected functional measures with high-intensity laser added to spinal decompression, but not a significant pain advantage. A separate lumbar-herniation trial is related rather than direct evidence and found low-level laser similar to placebo on several outcomes. Trials isolating low-power PBM and reporting longer follow-up would clarify the category-specific effect.
